item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q010_rossmann_family_function_divergence","answer":"In the current SCOPe release 2.08, these are three different families—alcohol-dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domains c.2.1.1 (sunid 51736), CoA-binding domains c.2.1.8 (sunid 51900), and potassium-channel NAD-binding domains c.2.1.9 (sunid 63944)—within the same NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold superfamily c.2.1 (sunid 51735), Rossmann fold c.2 (sunid 51734), and alpha/beta class c. Sharing a superfamily is stronger than merely sharing a fold: SCOPe considers a remote common evolutionary origin probable, even where sequence similarity is weak. Their separation into different families means that close homology and detailed function are not established across the three groups. In particular, one must not transfer alcohol-dehydrogenase activity, CoA binding, NAD(P) specificity, potassium-channel regulation, catalytic residues, or ligand specificity from one family to another; even the Rossmann-superfamily name does not prove that every member binds NAD(P). A member of another c.2.1 family may serve as a remote template for the conserved domain core and topology, but family-matched templates are needed for binding-site geometry, insertions and loops, interfaces, oligomeric state, and multidomain or membrane-channel context. Representatives should therefore be selected separately for each family, with compatible domain boundaries and biological context, rather than treating one c.2.1 structure as representative of all three.
